sections.text: The data were collected at one moment in time. So the study cannot show which came first, or that one link causes the next. It only shows that these things go together. Everything was self-reported. Most people in the sample were women, all had lived through something hard, and all were Turkish adults recruited online. In Türkiye, family, community and faith strongly shape meaning and views of death, so the pattern may look different elsewhere. Hatun also warns against one misreading: disliking uncertainty does not automatically ruin your life satisfaction.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: Struggling with the unknown is not a personal flaw. It is part of being human. What you can shape is the purpose you build around it.

recall.q: The study linked finding uncertainty hard to bear with lower life satisfaction. What two things sat in the middle of that chain, and why can't we say one caused the next?
recall.a: A weaker sense of meaning in life and a stronger fear of death. Intolerance of uncertainty went with weaker meaning, weaker meaning went with more fear of death, and more fear of death went with lower life satisfaction. The data came from one moment in time, so the study shows these things go together but cannot prove the order or the cause.

cards.title: The aging brain changes in three acts, a huge atlas shows
cards.body: Scientists read gene activity in 6.3 million brain cells from 1,494 people, from before birth to past 100. The brain changes fast until adulthood, then stays mostly still for decades. Around 60 a new wave of change begins. This time the brain's support cells lead it, not its neurons.
cards.evidence: cell atlas + 8 companion studies · n=1,494 postmortem brains · 6.3 million nuclei

sections.text:
The youngest brain in the collection had not yet been born. The oldest came from someone who lived past 100. In between were 1,494 people. From each one, scientists studied tissue from the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, an area at the front of the brain.

They did not study the tissue as one lump. They took out 6.3 million cell nuclei, one at a time. A nucleus is the core of a cell, where its genes are kept. For each one, they read which genes were switched on. Genes are instructions, so the active ones show what a cell is busy doing. The result is a brain-cell atlas that follows these patterns across a whole human life. It was published in Nature with eight companion studies. About half of the differences in the data came from cell type. The next biggest factor was simply which person the cells came from.

The atlas shows a life in three acts. The first act runs up to adulthood, and it is loud. The brain is still making new neurons and new glia, the support cells that look after neurons. Gene activity shifts a lot. The second act, from early adulthood through middle age, is strangely quiet. The patterns barely move. The third act starts at around 60. Change returns, and this time glia and immune cells lead it.

One detail from the late act stands out. The team looked at about 200 adults without brain disease. After 60, their clock genes, which keep the body's daily rhythm, were especially out of sync. But no one's sleep was measured. The researchers rebuilt these rhythms by comparing donors who died at different times of day. So this is a lead to follow, not a direct observation.

The atlas also covers people with brain disorders: 500 with Alzheimer's, 120 with schizophrenia, 55 with bipolar disorder, and others. In diseases like dementia, where brain cells break down, cells other than neurons made up a bigger share than usual. In mental illnesses, a group of neurons in the deep layers of the cortex, the brain's outer layer, was more common instead. Yet both groups changed some of the same genes. Many of these genes are basic to keeping any cell working. So Panos Roussos, one of the researchers, warns that studying each disorder alone can hide biology they share.

A model of how diseases progress added one more finding. As a disease gets worse, each cell type follows its own path, and that path is not a straight line. These changes may even shape how the disease unfolds.

Finally, 439 donors were of non-European or mixed ancestry. This kind of analysis has never covered people outside European groups at this scale before. Many of the cell-level mechanisms looked the same across ancestries.

sections.label: The caveat
sections.text: These brains were studied after death. What they show reflects a whole lifetime of experience, not one clear cause. Outside experts say atlases like this are best for building ideas to test and showing where to look next. They do not prove how a disease works. The clock-gene pattern was pieced together across different people, not measured inside any one person. And many population groups are still missing.

sections.label: Worth carrying
sections.text: The brain races while you grow, then holds still for decades. Around 60 it starts to change again, led by the cells that care for neurons.

recall.q: The atlas splits a life into three acts. What happens in the middle act, and what is different about the change that starts around 60?
recall.a: From early adulthood through middle age, gene activity in brain cells barely changes. Around 60, change returns, and it is led by glia and immune cells, the brain's support cells, not by neurons.
